title: Identifying redundant joins
objective: Spot joins whose columns are never used, joins used only as filters (replace with EXISTS / IN), and 'redundant' joins that secretly change the row set — then rewrite without changing the intended result.
context: Code review season. Half the queries in the shared repository join four tables to answer a one-table question. Each extra join costs compute, and some of them quietly drop rows (the orphan order 31) or duplicate them. Your job: simplify without changing what the business asked for.

exercises.title: Drop an unused LEFT JOIN
exercises.question: Review this: `SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, o.order_status FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('cancelled','pending')`.
exercises.prompt: Return the same result without the join: order_id, order_date, order_status for orders whose status is 'cancelled' or 'pending'.
hints: Which customers columns are used? None.
A LEFT JOIN on customers' primary key can neither add nor remove orders rows.
SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('cancelled','pending');
exercises.why: The simplest optimisation is deleting work. Unused LEFT JOINs to a unique key are pure cost.

recall.q: When is an unused LEFT JOIN guaranteed safe to remove?
recall.a: When the join key is unique on the joined table, so it cannot multiply rows (and LEFT never drops rows).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('cancelled','pending');

exercises.title: Join + DISTINCT → EXISTS
exercises.question: Review this: `SELECT DISTINCT o.order_id, o.order_date FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id WHERE p.category = 'Books'`.
exercises.prompt: Rewrite it with EXISTS (no DISTINCT needed) and return order_id and order_date of every order (any status) containing at least one product in category 'Books'.
hints: order_items and products are only used to decide WHETHER an order qualifies.
A semi-join (EXISTS) returns each order at most once.
SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON ... WHERE oi.order_id = o.order_id AND p.category = 'Books');
exercises.why: DISTINCT after a join is a red flag: the join multiplied rows you never wanted. EXISTS states the intent.

recall.a: It's a yes/no test per outer row — the outer row is returned at most once.

exercises.snowflake: Same EXISTS query; Snowflake plans it as a semi-join.

exercises.title: The 'redundant' join that was hiding a bug
exercises.question: Review this: `SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY oi.product_id`. No customers or products columns are used — but the customers INNER JOIN silently drops orphan order 31.
exercises.prompt: Remove the unused customers and products joins and return product_id and units_sold (sum of quantity) over ALL valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), including order 31 whose customer is missing.
hints: The orders join IS needed — it supplies order_status.
customers and products contribute no columns; the customers INNER JOIN removes order 31's lines.
SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN (...) GROUP BY oi.product_id;
exercises.why: Products 4 and 20 were under-reported by the old query because of order 31. Removing an INNER JOIN can *change* the result — here, it fixes it.

recall.q: Can removing an unused INNER JOIN change a query's result?
recall.a: Yes — the INNER JOIN filtered out rows without a match; removing it brings them back.

exercises.snowflake: Same; and if customers had a RELY foreign key from orders, Snowflake might have removed the join itself — giving the 'right' answer for the wrong reason.

exercises.title: LEFT JOIN + IS NOT NULL → semi-join
exercises.question: Review this: `SELECT DISTINCT o.order_id, o.customer_id FROM orders o LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id LEFT JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id WHERE r.return_id IS NOT NULL`.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id and customer_id for every order that has at least one returned line (a returns row on one of its order_items), written as a semi-join (EXISTS or IN) without DISTINCT.
hints: LEFT JOIN followed by WHERE right.col IS NOT NULL is just an INNER JOIN in disguise.
And since only orders columns are output, it's really an existence test.
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi JOIN returns r ON r.order_item_id = oi.order_item_id WHERE oi.order_id = o.order_id);
exercises.why: Today no order has two returned lines, so the DISTINCT happens to be harmless — but the first order with two returns would need it. A semi-join can never duplicate an order, so the query stays correct as the data grows.

recall.q: What does `LEFT JOIN t ... WHERE t.key IS NOT NULL` amount to?
recall.a: An INNER JOIN (the unmatched rows the LEFT JOIN kept are filtered away).

exercises.title: Keep the filter join, drop the decoration join
exercises.question: Review this: `SELECT oi.order_id, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price),2) AS gross_value FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY oi.order_id`. Products 21 (supplier 9 doesn't exist) and 22 (NULL supplier) make the suppliers join drop lines.
exercises.prompt: Return order_id and gross_value (SUM(quantity * unit_price) of ALL the order's lines, rounded to 2 decimals) for every valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) that has lines. Use orders only as a filter (EXISTS or IN) and do not join products or suppliers.
hints: products/suppliers are never output — but the INNER JOIN to suppliers drops lines for products 21 and 22.
orders is needed only to test the status → IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE ...).
SELECT oi.order_id, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price),2) AS gross_value FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.order_id IN (SELECT ...) GROUP BY oi.order_id;
exercises.why: Chains of 'decoration' joins accumulate in shared queries. Each INNER JOIN to a dimension with imperfect keys is a silent filter on your revenue.

recall.q: Which lines did the suppliers INNER JOIN drop?
recall.a: Lines for product 21 (supplier 9 doesn't exist) and product 22 (NULL supplier_id).

exercises.snowflake: Same query; `WHERE oi.order_id IN (SELECT ...)` becomes a semi-join in the plan.

exercises.title: Anti-join instead of LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY + HAVING
exercises.question: Review this: `SELECT c.customer_id, c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name HAVING COUNT(oi.order_item_id) = 0`.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id and name of customers who have no valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')), written with NOT EXISTS and without joining order_items. (Every valid order has lines, so this is the same set.)
hints: 'Customers with no X' is an anti-join.
The order_items join and the GROUP BY/HAVING only existed to count to zero.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN (...));
exercises.why: Customer 16 only has a cancelled order — the status condition belongs inside the NOT EXISTS, which is far easier to read than an ON-clause filter plus HAVING COUNT(...) = 0.

recall.q: Why prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN (subquery)?
recall.a: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields a NULL; NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe.

worked_example.question: Does the INNER JOIN to customers in this count change the answer? `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id`
worked_example.sql:
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders)                                  AS orders_alone,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c
                ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id)                       AS with_inner_join,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c
                ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id)                       AS with_left_join;
worked_example.explanation: No customer column is used, yet the INNER JOIN drops order 31 (customer 99 doesn't exist): 59 vs 60. The LEFT JOIN on customers' primary key is truly redundant (60 = 60). 'Unused' does not mean 'harmless' — check the row count before and after removing a join.

recipe:
**Recipe: audit every join with 3 questions**

1. **Is any column of the joined table used** in SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING or ORDER BY? If no → candidate for removal.
2. **Can the join change the row count?**
   - LEFT JOIN on the joined table's primary key → never changes rows → safe to remove if unused.
   - INNER JOIN → may **drop** rows without a match (orphans!) → removing it *adds* rows back. Decide which is right.
   - Join to a "many" side (e.g. order_items) → may **multiply** rows → removing it changes counts/sums.
3. **Is it only a filter?** ("orders that have a Books item") → use `EXISTS` / `IN` — no duplicates, no DISTINCT needed.

```sql
-- before: join + DISTINCT just to filter
SELECT DISTINCT o.order_id FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.category = 'Books';
-- after: semi-join
SELECT o.order_id FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
              WHERE oi.order_id = o.order_id AND p.category = 'Books');
```
snowflake_notes:
- Snowflake's optimizer can eliminate some redundant joins automatically **only when it knows the keys are
  unique and matching** — and Snowflake does *not enforce* PRIMARY KEY / FOREIGN KEY / UNIQUE constraints.
  You can declare them with the `RELY` property so the optimizer may trust them:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ADD CONSTRAINT pk_customers PRIMARY KEY (customer_id) RELY;
ALTER TABLE orders    ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer
      FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (customer_id) RELY;
```
  With RELY, an unused LEFT JOIN to `customers` (and even an INNER JOIN, given a RELY foreign key) can be
  removed by the optimizer. If the data violates the constraint (order 31!), results can be wrong — so only
  declare RELY on keys you test (Lesson 49).
- Semi-joins: `WHERE EXISTS (...)`, `WHERE x IN (SELECT ...)`; anti-joins: `NOT EXISTS`. Beware
  `NOT IN (subquery)` when the subquery can return NULL — it returns no rows at all.
- In dbt, wide "mega-models" that join every dimension are a common source of redundant joins; select from the
  narrowest model that has the columns you need.
common_mistakes: Assuming an unused INNER JOIN is harmless — it filters out non-matching rows (orphans, NULL keys).
Using DISTINCT to clean up duplicates created by a join that should have been EXISTS.
Removing a join that is actually used in WHERE/GROUP BY/ORDER BY (search the whole query, not just SELECT).
Writing NOT IN (subquery) where the subquery can return NULL.
Declaring RELY constraints in Snowflake on keys that are actually violated — the optimizer will trust them.
recall: Three questions to ask about every join?
Are its columns used? Can it drop or multiply rows? Is it only a filter (→ EXISTS)?
Semi-join (EXISTS/IN) keeps rows that have a match; anti-join (NOT EXISTS) keeps rows that don't.
Does Snowflake enforce PRIMARY KEY / FOREIGN KEY constraints?
No (except NOT NULL); they're metadata, optionally trusted by the optimizer with RELY.
